faqs: What should I wear for HYROX Cancun in February heat and humidity?

Race in a tech shirt like the Compromised Running tee (APC-C36, $38) or Push Heavy. Run Fast. shirt (APC-C40, $38). Use the Apex AeroShell Lightweight Race Warmup Jacket (APC-C42, $68) only in the start corral, then strip it 60-90 seconds before the horn so you do not carry soaked fabric into Run 1.
How do I pack for Cancun race weekend without overpacking?

Carry race kit, backup socks, electrolyte powder, and a packable shell in the 8-Station Race Day 50L All-Weather Gym & Shoe Duffle (APC-C14, $74). Keep carbon racers in the ventilated shoe tunnel so turf chalk and sand from Malecón warmups do not wreck the uppers overnight.
How many days of heat acclimation do I need before Cancun?

Aim for 7-10 days of Zone 2 work in warm conditions or heated indoor sessions if you live in a cold climate. Keep long runs easy, practice Roxzone shuffles in humidity, and do one short station session in race gear so you learn how the fabric feels when saturated.
Is the Miami Beach Heat-Block tee useful for Cancun even though it is a different city?

Yes for heat culture and training days. The Miami Beach Heat-Block South Florida Endurance Club tee (APC-C19, $38) is a heavyweight city crest piece for travel, expo, and easy sessions. For the race itself, prefer Compromised Running or Push Heavy so humidity does not trap heat against your torso.
guides.body_html:
Why Cancun Heat Hits Differently Than Indoor Convention-Center Waves

HYROX Cancun at Malecón Tajamar (February 2027) is not the same thermal problem as Chicago Navy Pier or Dallas Kay Bailey Hutchison. Coastal humidity, reflective pavement, and open-air staging raise wet-bulb stress even when the thermometer looks "only" mid-70s to mid-80s F. Athletes who copy a cold-city corral plan - heavy hoodie, late strip, aggressive Run 1 - usually pay for it by Station 3 with early heart-rate drift and sticky fabric that never dries between 1km loops.

This guide covers race-week apparel, packing, heat acclimation, start-corral layering, and post-race cool-down so you treat Cancun as a humidity race first and a strength race second. Product links below go to live Apex Hybrid Co pages; prices match the current catalog.

Race Kit Hierarchy: Vented Base, Packable Shell, Dry Bag

Build three layers of intent:

  • Race base: Compromised Running (APC-C36) or Push Heavy. Run Fast. (APC-C40) - both $38. Compromised Running favors laser-vent airflow on compromised 1km runs; Push Heavy favors durability when sandbag and sled contact soak the torso.
  • Corral shell: Apex AeroShell Lightweight Race Warmup Jacket (APC-C42) at $68. Wear it for pulse-raiser strides and thoracic mobility, then strip and stow before the horn so you do not start Run 1 in a windbreaker that traps Cancun humidity.
  • Travel / expo piece: Miami Beach Heat-Block South Florida Endurance Club (APC-C19) at $38 for walk-around days, expo photos, and easy Zone 2. Save the lightest tech shirt for race morning.

Optional swap for athletes who run very hot: Zone 5 Engine Zone 4 / Zone 5 Engine (APC-C38) or Roxzone Speed Dept. (APC-C41) - both $38 - for high-ventilation training blocks in the week before race day.

Travel Packing for Malecón Tajamar Weekend

Fly with a single organized bag so hotel chaos does not cost you sleep. The 8-Station Race Day 50L All-Weather Gym & Shoe Duffle (APC-C14) at $74 keeps carbon racers in a ventilated shoe tunnel and separates wet towels from dry race kit. Pack checklist:

  • Primary race tee + backup identical size (humidity + chalk can ruin a shirt overnight)
  • AeroShell packed flat; do not check it if you need it for a cool morning corral
  • 2-3 pairs of race socks, balm, electrolyte sachets, sunscreen stick
  • Cheap hotel flip-flops for post-race cool-down walks; keep race shoes dry
  • Light recovery layer for AC-blasted restaurants after you finish soaked

Heat Acclimation Window (7-10 Days)

If you live in a cold climate, do not invent a crash sauna plan three days out. Prefer progressive exposure:

  1. Days -10 to -7: Easy Zone 2 outdoors or in a warm gym in race-kit fabric. Cap intensity. Goal is sweating in the shirt you will race in.
  2. Days -6 to -4: One short hybrid session (sled or wall-ball effort + 1km repeats) in Compromised Running or Push Heavy. Practice drinking on a schedule, not by thirst alone.
  3. Days -3 to -1: Reduce volume. Keep brief heat exposure so the system stays primed. Sleep, sodium, and arrival hydration matter more than another hard station day.

On arrival, walk Malecón in the evening heat with an easy pulse so your body maps the local humidity before wave day. Avoid all-day beach sunburn the day before your heat - burned skin raises perceived exertion.

Start-Corral Layering on a Humid Morning

Treat the corral like a short runway, not a fashion show:

  • Arrive already in race base + AeroShell.
  • 8 minutes easy jog / shuffle if space allows; otherwise march in place with high cadence.
  • Dynamic hips and ankles; keep arms loose for farmer-carry and wall-ball positions later.
  • Strip AeroShell 60-90 seconds before the horn. Hand it to a friend or stage it in your duffle plan - do not invent a late drop that makes you miss the wave.

If the morning breeze feels cool on bare arms, that is usually fine in Cancun. Overdressing for "feeling cold" is how athletes enter Run 1 already damp.

During-Race Humidity Management

Prioritize Roxzone movement over standing recovery. Short-stride shuffle to the next station keeps blood moving without a hard acceleration. Sip on a schedule at aid if available; do not chug a full bottle right before sled push. If fabric starts clinging, resist the urge to constantly tug the hem - that wastes seconds and attention. Choose the vented shirt before the race so you do not negotiate with cotton mid-event.

Post-Race Cool-Down Without Crashing

After the finish, get shade, walk 8-10 minutes, and change into a dry shirt from the duffle before AC and ice baths. A sudden cold blast on a still-racing heart rate feels good for 30 seconds and then leaves you shivering and depleted. Rehydrate with electrolytes, eat a simple carb + protein meal within 90 minutes, and keep the AeroShell for the walk back to the hotel if evening wind picks up.

guides.title: Roxzone Transition Drills - Cut Dead Time Between the 8 Stations (Gear Drops, Breathing, Line Choice, Doubles)
guides.summary: Practice drills that shrink dead time between HYROX stations - gear drops, breathing resets, line choice, and doubles handoffs - with Roxzone Speed Dept., Roxzone Penalties, Compromised Running, 1km Split, and Run. Station. Repeat. training pieces.
faqs: What is the fastest way to practice Roxzone transitions?

Run short station-to-station drills 2x per week: finish a station effort, immediately hit a 15-20 second high-cadence shuffle, reset breathing for 3 breaths, then start the next station. Wear a light tech shirt like Roxzone Speed Dept. (APC-C41, $38) so fabric drag does not teach bad habits.
How should doubles partners practice handoffs?

Rehearse verbal cues and physical tags at walking pace first, then at race shuffle. Agree who carries chalk, who leads line choice, and who speaks first at crowded stations. Matching kits like Run. Station. Repeat. (APC-C01, $38) help partners spot each other in a busy Roxzone.
Do Roxzone drills replace compromised running work?

No. Drills cut dead time; compromised 1km sessions still build the engine. Pair transition drills after lighter station work, then keep one quality 1km day in Compromised Running (APC-C36, $38) or 1km Split (APC-C37, $38) each week.
Why do athletes still lose time after they "know" they should hustle?

Knowing is not a motor pattern. Without reps, the nervous system defaults to walking after hard stations. The Roxzone Penalties Ruined My PR tee (APC-C23, $38) is a cue; the drill calendar is the fix.
guides.body_html:
Dead Time Is a Training Problem, Not a Motivation Problem

Most athletes already know they should not stroll through the Roxzone. They still lose 15-40 seconds per station because the walk is automatic after a hard sled, ski, or wall-ball set. The fix is not another race-day pep talk. The fix is rehearsed transitions that make the shuffle, breath reset, and line choice the default under fatigue.

This guide is a drill library. Use it in gym Roxzone simulations and open-floor hybrid sessions. Pair it with breathable race fabric so the practice feels like race day: Roxzone Speed Dept. (APC-C41), Roxzone Penalties Ruined My PR (APC-C23), Compromised Running (APC-C36), 1km Split (APC-C37), and Run. Station. Repeat. (APC-C01) - tech shirts $38.

Drill 1: Gear Drop to Shuffle (15-20 Seconds)

Purpose: kill the post-station freeze.

  • Finish a station effort (example: 20 wall balls or a short sled push).
  • Drop or rack the implement cleanly - no theatrical celebration.
  • Within one second, hit a short-stride shuffle at roughly 170-180 steps per minute for 15-20 seconds toward a taped "out" line.
  • Stop, note how many seconds you wasted before the first shuffle step. Repeat 6-8 times.

Cue: eyes up, hips tall, arms quiet. If you always walk the first five steps, film one set and watch it once - the feedback is usually enough.

Drill 2: Three-Breath Reset While Moving

Standing still to "catch your breath" often costs more than a controlled shuffle with nasal-to-mouth breathing. Practice:

  1. After the station, start the shuffle immediately.
  2. Take three deliberate breaths on a rhythm (example: inhale 2 steps, exhale 2 steps).
  3. On breath three, scan the next station line and commit to an entry path.

Do this when heart rate is high. Calm breathing only in a rested state does not transfer. Roxzone Speed Dept. (APC-C41) is a good training shirt here because it stays out of the way when you are already hot.

Drill 3: Line Choice Rehearsals

Crowded stations punish indecision. Build a simple decision tree and practice it:

  • If the nearest lane has 2+ athletes waiting and a farther lane is open, take the open lane without apologizing to the floor.
  • If all lanes are stacked, join the shortest queue and stay ready - chalk hands while waiting if your station needs it.
  • Never reverse direction in the Roxzone unless safety requires it; U-turns create collisions and penalties risk.

Gym version: set three tape boxes as fake stations with cones as "occupied" markers. Finish a burpee set, shuffle, and pick a box under a 5-second decision clock.

Drill 4: Doubles Handoffs Under Fatigue

Doubles teams lose time on unclear ownership. Practice with the same verbal script every time:

  • Tag + call: physical tag on the shoulder plus a one-word call ("GO" / "YOURS").
  • Tool custody: decide who carries chalk, belt, or spare grips before the session - not mid-Roxzone.
  • Lead / trail: one athlete always leads line choice; the other mirrors without debating.

Run three fatigued handoff reps after a shared station (example: shared wall balls). Matching Run. Station. Repeat. (APC-C01) or a sleeveless Run. Station. Repeat. Race Day tank (APC-C28, $32) makes visual tracking easier in a busy floor. Keep calls short; long sentences vanish under noise.

Weekly Microcycle (Two Short Sessions)

Session A (12-15 min): Gear-drop shuffle + three-breath reset after light station work. Shirt: 1km Split (APC-C37) or Compromised Running (APC-C36).

Session B (15-20 min): Line-choice cones + doubles handoffs if you race with a partner. Shirt: Roxzone Speed Dept. (APC-C41) or Roxzone Penalties (APC-C23) as a behavioral cue.

Keep these after skill work, not after a full race simulation every time. Fresh pattern learning beats sloppy late-session chaos.

What Not to Do

  • Do not practice transitions only on race week. Motor patterns need repetition.
  • Do not sprint the Roxzone from a dead stop after max-effort stations - that spikes HR and invites form collapse on the next run.
  • Do not debate line choice mid-shuffle. Decide, commit, adjust only for safety.
  • Do not treat funny penalty shirts as a substitute for drills. APC-C23 is a reminder; the stopwatch still wants reps.

Transfer Test

Once every two weeks, run a mini circuit: Ski or row effort -> shuffle drill -> short sled or lunges -> shuffle drill -> wall balls -> shuffle drill. Time total dead time between stations with a simple phone timer. If dead time drops across weeks while station quality holds, the drills are working.

Athletes who warm up in heavy 14 oz fleece hoodies soak their base layer in sweat before entering the start corral - or worse, stand cold in a singlet for 20 minutes and hit the first 1,000m run with vasoconstricted quads and stiff ankles.

Start with 6–8 minutes of easy conversational jogging (125–135 BPM) in your Apex AeroShell Lightweight Race Warmup Jacket (APC-C42) or Hybrid 8-Station Windbreaker Track Jacket (APC-C43). Pair this with 2 sets of 15 breaths on the AeroLung Dual-Valve Resistance Breathing Trainer. Pre-activating the diaphragm delays the inspiratory metaboreflex - the physiological trigger that steals blood flow from your legs during Station 01 SkiErg and Station 02 Sled Push.

  • Ankle & Tibialis Prep (for Sled Push & Wall Balls): 15 knee-to-wall dorsiflexion pulses per side so your heels stay planted during heavy sled drives and Station 08 squats.

Phase 3: T-Minus 8 Minutes - Lactate Priming Strides & Corral Shed

Run three 20-second progressive strides at your target 1,000m race pace with 60 seconds of walking recovery. These short bursts upregulate oxidative enzymes so Kilometer 1 feels controlled rather than shocking. Keep your 26/27 World Series Lightweight Warmup Jacket (APC-C45) zipped until 90 seconds before the corral countdown, then stow it in your drop bag and step to the line dry and thermoregulated in your Apex Compromised Running 4.0 Breathable Race Tech Tee (APC-C36).

guides.summary: A data-backed pacing calculator and biomechanical blueprint for all eight 1,000m runs - how to survive Run 3 after the heavy sled push, lock cadence at 180 SPM, and eliminate Roxzone bleed.
faqs: What should my 1,000m compromised running pace be compared to my open 10K pace?

Your target compromised 1,000m split should be 8 to 15 seconds per kilometer slower than your standalone open 10K pace. Going out at open 5K pace on Run 1 spikes blood lactate above 6 mmol/L before the sleds and costs 3–5 minutes across Runs 5 through 8.
How do I stop my legs from locking up on the run immediately after Sled Push and Lunges?

For the first 200 meters leaving the Roxzone after Station 02 (Sled Push) and Station 07 (Sandbag Lunges), shorten your stride by 10–15% and spin a quick 180+ SPM cadence while keeping your torso stacked. Within 250 meters, venous return flushes local hydrogen ions and allows you to lengthen back to race stride.
guides.body_html:
53% of Your Total Race Time Happens on the 1,000m Track

In an 8-station hybrid race, the eight 1,000m runs account for more than half of your total clock time - yet most athletes train stations in isolation and treat the runs as recovery jogs. When you exit Station 02 (50m Heavy Sled Push) and Station 03 (50m Sled Pull), intramuscular pressure and localized quad acidosis alter your ground-contact mechanics. Mastering compromised running is the fastest way to drop 4+ minutes off your personal best.

The 8×1,000m Split Pacing Matrix

  • Run 01 (Pre-SkiErg): Run at Target Pace + 3 seconds. Stay capped below 86% max HR on your PulsePro ANT+ & Bluetooth Chest-Strap Heart Rate Monitor.
  • Run 02 (Post-SkiErg): Settle directly into Target Pace. Upper-body lats and triceps are taxed, so relax your shoulders in the 1km Split 1KM Split Tech Tee (APC-C37).
  • Run 03 & Run 04 (Post-Sled Push & Sled Pull): The danger zone. Use a short, high-cadence shuffle for the first 200m out of the Roxzone arch, then build back to Target Pace + 5 seconds.
  • Run 06, 07 & 08 (The Championship Back Half): Where races are won. Athletes wearing the Apex Compromised Running 4.0 Breathable Tech Tee (APC-C36) or train negative-split Brick intervals every Sunday so Run 08 is their fastest split of the day.

The 200-Meter Post-Sled Cadence Reset

Never walk out of the Roxzone. Walking drops intramuscular muscle-pump action, leaving metabolites pooled in the vastus medialis. Instead, jog immediately at a compact 180 SPM cadence for 45 seconds until your stride opens up naturally.

guides.title: Station 8 Wall Balls: How to Go Unbroken on Your Final 100 Reps

Two reasons: hip crease failing to break parallel (90°) when quads are cramped after Station 07 Sandbag Lunges, and the medicine ball grazing below the center of the 3.0m (men) / 2.7m (women) target. Improving ankle dorsiflexion with the Tibialis Trainer Bar keeps your torso upright at full depth.

Station 08 Is Where Podiums and Sub-65 Qualifiers Are Decided

Arriving at the Station 08 Wall Ball rig after 8,000 meters of running and 100 meters of sandbag lunges is the ultimate test of neuromuscular efficiency. A single no-rep for shallow squat depth or a low target strike wastes precious energy when your anterior deltoids and quads are already redlined.

1. Fix Your Squat Depth Before Race Week: Ankle Dorsiflexion & Thoracic Extension

When ankle dorsiflexion is restricted, your heels lift or your torso pitches forward at the bottom of the squat - forcing your lower back and shoulders to heave the 6kg/9kg ball from a terrible angle. Spend 5 minutes before every lower-body session on the Tibialis Anterior Trainer Bar and mobilize your upper back on the VibeRoll Pro 4-Speed Vibrating Foam Roller so you can catch the ball in a stacked front-rack position.

2. Overhead Freedom: Eliminate Shoulder Pinch on Reps 60–100

Standard cotton sleeves bind across the wet deltoid after 60 minutes of sweating, adding subtle resistance on every overhead throw. That is why elite racers compete in the deep-cut 100 Wall Balls Unbroken Sleeveless Muscle Tank (APC-C31) or warm up in the 100 Wall Balls Unbroken* Heavyweight Tee (APC-C03) and Wall Balls & Bad Decisions Heavyweight Hoodie (APC-C10).

3. The Championship 100-Rep Pacing Blueprint

  • Competitive Open Division (5 Sets): 25 – 20 – 20 – 20 – 15 reps. Let your arms drop completely as the ball travels upward to flush shoulder capillaries between every catch.

guides.title: SkiErg & RowErg 1000m Pacing: Split Targets That Save Your Legs for the Next Run
guides.summary: How to pick a sustainable /500m split for the 1000m SkiErg and RowErg stations, why the first 200m decides your next kilometer, and the simple damper and stroke-rate settings that keep your heart rate in check.
faqs: What /500m split should I hold on a 1000m SkiErg in a hybrid race?

A good starting point is roughly 8 to 12 seconds slower per 500m than your best 1000m time trial. If your fresh 1000m ski is 3:50 (about 1:55/500m), aim for something close to 2:03 to 2:07 on race day so you can still run the next kilometer at your target pace.
What damper setting should I use on the RowErg?

Most hybrid racers do well between 4 and 6. A higher damper feels stronger but loads your legs and lower back early, which you'll pay for on the sled and lunges later. Check the drag factor in the monitor's menu and set it the same way every training session.
Should I go out hard on the first erg station?

No. The first station comes right after your first run, when adrenaline is highest. Hold your planned split for the first 200m, then settle in. Going out 10 seconds too fast per 500m usually costs far more time on the next run than it saves on the erg.
guides.body_html:
The SkiErg and RowErg look like the easy stations. You're not carrying anything, nobody is judging your reps, and the screen tells you exactly how fast you're going. That's precisely why so many people blow up on them. It's easy to chase a number in the first 200 meters and then spend the next run wondering why your legs feel like concrete.

This guide is about choosing a split you can actually hold, and keeping enough in the tank that the run out of the station feels normal.

Start with a fresh 1000m test

Once a month, do a fresh 1000m time trial on each erg after a proper warm-up. Write down the average /500m split. That number is your ceiling, not your race pace. On race day you'll be arriving with a hard kilometer already in your legs and a full race still ahead.

As a rule of thumb, add about 8 to 12 seconds per 500m to your fresh test for the SkiErg, and about 6 to 10 seconds for the RowErg. Newer racers should sit at the slower end of that range. If you're chasing a podium in your age group, test the faster end in a full simulation before you commit to it.

The first 200 meters decide everything

Your heart rate lags behind your effort. For the first 30 to 40 seconds, a pace that's far too fast still feels fine. By the time your watch catches up, the damage is done. Pick your target split before you walk into the station and hold it from the very first pull, even if it feels almost too easy.

A simple cue that works: count your first 10 strokes calmly, check the screen, and adjust. Don't look at the person next to you.

SkiErg: use your hips, spare your arms

On the ski, the power should come from a hip hinge and a small knee bend, with your arms finishing the stroke near your thighs. If your triceps and lats are on fire halfway through, you're pulling with your arms. Stand a little taller, let the handles rise fully overhead, and drop your body weight into each pull.

Stroke rate for most people lands somewhere between 40 and 50 strokes per minute at race effort. Long, heavy strokes at a lower rate tend to be cheaper on the heart than a frantic fast rate.

RowErg: leg drive first, and don't crank the damper

The row is the only station where you get to sit down, which tempts people to treat it as a rest. It isn't. But it also isn't the place to win the race. Keep the damper around 4 to 6, drive with your legs, then swing your body back, then finish with the arms. Recover in the opposite order.

A stroke rate of roughly 24 to 30 per minute is a comfortable race range for most hybrid athletes. If your split drops as soon as you raise the rate, your stroke is getting short. Slow the rate down and lengthen the drive.

Practice the transition, not just the erg

The real test is the first 300 meters of running after you climb off. Build workouts that pair them directly, for example 4 rounds of 500m SkiErg at race split straight into a 1km run at goal pace, with 2 minutes easy between rounds. You'll learn quickly whether your planned split leaves your legs ready to run.

Wear something that doesn't trap heat for these sessions. Our 1km Split Threshold Tech Tee is a lightweight option, and if you train in a cold garage, the Erg Doesn't Care How You Feel Fleece Hoodie is made for warm-ups before you peel it off. Keep fluids close with the insulated shaker bottle.

A simple race-day plan

Before the race, write two numbers on your hand or set them on your watch: your SkiErg target split and your RowErg target split. Hold them, finish each station feeling like you could do another 200m, and let the runs be where you make up time. The athletes who look smooth on the erg screens are usually the ones who look smooth on the last kilometer too.

guides.title: Zone 2 Heart Rate Training With a Chest Strap: A 12-Week Base Plan for Hybrid Racers
guides.summary: Why a chest strap is more reliable than a wrist sensor for Zone 2, three simple ways to find your zone, and a 12-week aerobic base plan that builds the engine you need for eight runs and eight stations.
faqs: Why use a chest strap instead of a watch for Zone 2 training?

A chest strap reads the electrical signal from your heart, while most watches estimate heart rate with light through the skin. Wrist sensors can drift during arm-heavy work like the SkiErg, rowing, or carries, and in cold weather. For staying inside a narrow Zone 2 band, a strap is usually more consistent.
How do I find my Zone 2 heart rate?

The most practical options are a lab or field lactate test, a percentage of a measured threshold heart rate (roughly 80 to 89 percent of lactate threshold heart rate), or the talk test: you should be able to speak in full sentences while breathing through your nose. Formulas based only on age are a rough starting point at best.
How much Zone 2 should a hybrid racer do each week?

Many athletes do well with about 70 to 80 percent of their weekly training time at easy aerobic effort, with the rest spent on threshold runs, race-pace intervals, and strength. Beginners can start with two or three 30 to 45 minute Zone 2 sessions per week and build from there.
guides.body_html:
Ask anyone who has finished a hybrid race what they wish they'd trained more, and you'll hear the same answer over and over: the engine. Eight kilometers of running broken up by eight stations is a long aerobic event. Strength matters, but the athletes who hold their pace on the last few runs are almost always the ones with a deep aerobic base.

Zone 2 training is the most reliable way to build that base. The catch is that Zone 2 is a narrow band, and it's surprisingly easy to drift above it without noticing. That's where a chest strap earns its place.

Why a chest strap beats the wrist for this

Most watches estimate heart rate by shining light through your skin. That works fine for steady running, but it can lag or jump around during arm-heavy work like the SkiErg, rowing, or farmer carries, and when it's cold or your watch band is loose. A chest strap reads the electrical signal from your heart directly, so the number you see is the number you're actually at.

When your whole session depends on staying under a ceiling, a reading that's off by 8 to 10 beats can turn an easy day into a moderate one. Do that four times a week and you're no longer doing base training.

Three ways to find your zone

Lactate testing. The most accurate option. A coach or sports lab measures your blood lactate at increasing paces, and your Zone 2 ceiling sits just below the point where lactate starts to rise.

Threshold heart rate. Run a hard, evenly paced 30 minutes solo and take your average heart rate for the last 20 minutes. That's a decent estimate of your lactate threshold heart rate. Zone 2 usually lands around 80 to 89 percent of it.

The talk test. If you can speak in full sentences and breathe comfortably through your nose, you're probably in the right place. It's free and surprisingly accurate. Use it alongside the strap to double-check the numbers.

Age-based formulas like 180 minus your age are fine for a first week, but they can be off by a lot for any individual. Test, then adjust.

A 12-week base plan

Weeks 1 to 4. Three Zone 2 sessions a week, 30 to 45 minutes each. Mix running with the bike or rower so your legs aren't pounded every day. Keep your normal strength sessions, but skip hard intervals for now.

Weeks 5 to 8. Stretch one session to 60 to 75 minutes. Add one threshold workout per week, such as 4 x 8 minutes at a comfortably hard pace with 2 minutes easy. Everything else stays easy.

Weeks 9 to 12. Keep the long Zone 2 day and the threshold day. Replace one easy session with a race-style workout: 1km runs at goal pace with a short station in between. Watch how quickly your heart rate settles on the runs. That recovery speed is the clearest sign the base is working.

What it feels like when it's working

The first few weeks often feel frustratingly slow. You may need to walk hills to stay under your ceiling. That's normal. Over a couple of months, your easy pace at the same heart rate should get faster, and your heart rate on race-pace work should come down more quickly between efforts.

Gear that helps on long easy days

Long, easy sessions are where comfort counts. The Zone 5 Engine Breathable Conditioning Tee stays light when the sun comes out, and the Zone 2 Engine Lab Cap keeps sweat out of your eyes. If you head out at dawn, layer the AeroShell Lightweight Warmup Jacket over the top and stash it once you warm up. And if you want a shirt that says exactly what your training week looks like, the Zone 2 All Week, Redline Weekend Tee was made for you.

Slow down on the easy days, so the hard days and race day can be fast.

guides.title: Burpee Broad Jumps Pacing Guide: Technique, Breathing and Rhythm for the 80m Station
guides.summary: How to set a steady rep rhythm, step back instead of jumping back, breathe on every rep, and leave the 80m burpee broad jump station with enough legs left for the next run.
faqs: How many burpee broad jumps does 80 meters take?

Most athletes land somewhere between 30 and 60 reps, depending on height and jump length. A long, efficient jump cuts reps, but chasing maximum distance on every rep burns your legs fast. A comfortable, repeatable jump is usually faster overall.
Is it faster to step back or jump back on burpee broad jumps?

Jumping both feet back is quicker on a single rep, but stepping back one foot at a time keeps your heart rate lower and saves your hip flexors. Many age-group racers jump back for the first third, then switch to stepping once breathing gets heavy.
How should I breathe during burpee broad jumps?

Pick one breath pattern and repeat it every rep, such as an exhale on the way down and a big inhale as you stand and swing your arms. Holding your breath on the floor is the most common reason the station falls apart halfway through.
guides.body_html:
The burpee broad jump station looks simple on paper: drop to the floor, stand up, jump forward, repeat for 80 meters. In practice it's the place where a lot of race plans quietly fall apart. It comes right after the sled pull, your legs are already loaded, and the movement asks for a full-body effort on every single rep.

The good news is that this station rewards rhythm much more than raw power. You don't need the longest jump in the field. You need a rep you can repeat 40 or 50 times without your heart rate climbing out of control.

Find a jump you can repeat, not your best jump

The instinct is to launch every jump as far as you can. Those big jumps cost a lot of leg energy and usually mean a slower, sloppier landing. A moderate jump, roughly the length of your own height or a little less, lands you balanced and ready to drop straight into the next rep.

In training, time yourself over 20 meters twice: once with maximum jumps, once with a comfortable, smooth jump. Most people find the smooth version is close in time and leaves them far fresher.

Step back or jump back?

Jumping both feet back is fast on one rep, but it spikes your heart rate and fatigues your hip flexors, which you still need for three more runs, the lunges and the wall balls. Stepping back one foot at a time is a few tenths slower per rep and a lot cheaper.

A sensible plan for most age-group racers is to jump back for the first third of the station while you're fresh, then switch to stepping back as soon as your breathing gets ragged. Practice both so the switch feels natural on race day.

Breathe on every single rep

Pick one breathing pattern and stick to it. A simple option is to exhale as you go down to the floor and take a big inhale as you stand and swing your arms for the jump. The worst habit is holding your breath on the floor, which leaves you gasping after ten reps.

If you need a reset, take it standing up, not lying down. Two slow breaths on your feet, then go again.

Set a rhythm and count it

Break the distance into chunks. Many racers count sets of 5 reps and allow one breath between sets. Others pick a landmark, like every two lane lines. Either way, the goal is to never fully stop. Steady movement wins this station.

A simple training block

Week 1 to 2. 4 rounds of 10 burpee broad jumps with a 400m easy run between rounds. Focus on smooth landings.

Week 3 to 4. 3 rounds of 20 reps, each followed by a 1km run at goal race pace. Note how your first 200 meters of running feel.

Week 5 to 6. A full 80m effort straight after a sled pull or heavy rowing piece, then a 1km run. This is the closest you'll get to the real sequence.

Get off the floor and run

The run after this station feels awful for almost everyone. Shorten your stride for the first 200 meters, let your breathing settle, then build back to race pace. Trying to make up time right away usually costs more later.

Gear that helps on burpee day

You'll spend a lot of time on the floor, so wear something that won't ride up or trap heat. The Push Heavy Breathable Turf & Sled Conditioning Tee stays light and dry through high-rep work. For the warmup and the walk home, the Burpee Broad Jumps Build Character Warmup Hoodie is made for exactly this station, and the Burpee Broad Jumps Build Character says what everyone in the gym is thinking. Keep electrolytes close between sessions with the 24oz Insulated Shaker Bottle.

Smooth beats heroic here. Find your rhythm, keep breathing, and save your legs for the second half of the race.

guides.title: Sandbag Lunges Station 7: Pacing, Posture and How to Save Your Legs for Wall Balls
guides.summary: How to carry the sandbag, keep an even lunge tempo over 100 meters, avoid the knee-touch no-reps that cost time, and train the lunge-to-wall-ball transition before race day.
faqs: How heavy is the sandbag for the lunge station?

In the standard format, Open men usually carry 20 kg and Open women 10 kg, while Pro men carry 30 kg and Pro women 20 kg. Always check the current rulebook for your event and division before race day, since weights can differ by division.
What is the best way to hold the sandbag during lunges?

Most racers carry it across the back of the shoulders, like a back squat position, because it keeps the chest up and frees the hips. Keep your hands wide on the bag and your elbows slightly down so it doesn't slide.
How do I keep my legs fresh for wall balls after the lunges?

Hold an even tempo instead of rushing the first 30 meters, take short standing pauses if you need them rather than long stops, and walk briskly through the transition to let your quads recover before the final run.
guides.body_html:
By the time you reach the sandbag lunges, you've already done six stations and seven runs. Your quads are tired, your grip is tired, and the wall balls are still waiting. The 100 meters of lunges aren't usually where people lose the most time, but they're where many people lose their legs for the finish.

The goal at this station is simple: get through cleanly, at an even pace, with as much left in your quads as possible.

Know the standard before you lunge

The back knee has to touch the ground on each rep, and you need to stand fully between lunges. No-reps are the hidden time cost here. A judge asking you to repeat reps adds seconds and extra fatigue you didn't plan for. Practice touching the knee lightly every time, so it becomes automatic.

Weights depend on division. In the standard format, Open men usually carry 20 kg and Open women 10 kg, while Pro men carry 30 kg and Pro women 20 kg. Check the current rulebook for your event.

Carry it high and stay tall

Most racers place the bag across the back of the shoulders, like a back squat. It keeps your chest up and lets your hips move freely. Hug the bag with your hands wide and your elbows slightly down. If the bag starts sliding, stop for one second and reset it. Fighting a slipping bag for 20 meters costs far more.

Keep your torso upright and your front shin roughly vertical. Leaning forward shifts the load onto your lower back and front knee, and it makes standing up much harder.

Pick a stride and a tempo

A comfortable stride length, roughly a normal walking step and a half, covers the ground well without stressing the hips. Then pick a tempo you could hold for the whole 100 meters, such as one lunge every two to three seconds.

The most common mistake is racing the first 30 meters. If you go out too fast, you'll be taking long breaks by the halfway mark. Even pacing almost always wins.

Break it before it breaks you

Plan short standing pauses in advance. For many age-group racers, a three-breath pause every 20 or 25 lunges works well. Keep the bag on your shoulders during the pause. Putting it down and picking it back up wastes time and energy.

Train the transition to wall balls

Lunges and wall balls both hammer the quads, with only the final run between them. Practice that exact sequence in training: 50 to 100 meters of lunges, a 1km run, then a set of 30 to 50 wall balls. Learn how your legs feel, and practice relaxing your stride on that last run so your quads can recover.

A simple progression. Start with 2 rounds of 50 meters of lunges with a moderate load, twice a week. Over four to six weeks, build to a full 100 meters at race weight, followed by the run and wall balls once a week.

Recovery after lunge-heavy sessions

Expect sore quads and glutes for a day or two after big lunge sessions. Easy cycling, light walking, and gentle mobility help more than total rest. Space your heaviest lunge day at least 48 hours from your hardest running session.

Gear for lunge day

A shirt that doesn't bunch under the sandbag makes a real difference. The 1km Split Lightweight Threshold Workout & Turf Tee sits flat and stays dry through long sets. If lunges feel personal, the Sandbag Lunges Are A Personal Attack Pump Cover says it for you, and the 200m Farmer Carry Survivors Club Tee covers the station right before it. Throw on the AeroShell Lightweight Warmup Jacket while you warm up and cool down.

Stay tall, stay steady, and save something for the wall balls.

guides.title: Cold Plunge vs. Sauna: Contrast Therapy Timing for Hybrid Athletes
guides.summary: When to use the sauna, when to use cold water, how long each round should last, and how to time contrast therapy around strength days, long runs and race week so it helps recovery instead of blunting your training.
faqs: Should I do the cold plunge or the sauna first?

For general recovery, most people start with heat and finish with cold, or alternate a few rounds and end on cold. If you want to sleep soon after, some athletes prefer to finish with a short warm shower so they aren't wired and shivering at bedtime.
How long should a cold plunge last after a workout?

For most people, 2 to 5 minutes in water around 10 to 15 °C (50 to 59 °F) is plenty. Longer and colder isn't automatically better, and you should get out right away if you feel numb, dizzy or start shivering hard.
Does a cold plunge hurt strength gains?

Research suggests regular cold-water immersion right after strength training can blunt some muscle-building adaptations. If strength is a priority, keep cold plunges at least 4 to 6 hours away from lifting sessions, or save them for running days and race week.
Is contrast therapy safe for everyone?

No. People with heart conditions, high or low blood pressure, Raynaud's, or who are pregnant should talk to a doctor before using saunas or cold plunges. Never use either after drinking alcohol, and always plunge with someone nearby.
guides.body_html:
Saunas and cold plunges have become a standard part of the hybrid training scene. Walk into almost any performance gym and you'll find people bouncing between the two after a heavy session. Both can help you feel better and recover between hard days, but the timing matters more than most people think.

This guide covers what each one actually does, how to structure a contrast session, and when to skip the cold so it doesn't get in the way of the fitness you're building.

What heat does

Sauna sessions raise your core temperature, increase heart rate and push blood toward the skin. Many athletes find regular sauna use relaxing and good for sleep, and some research links it to heat acclimation and better plasma volume, which can help in warm race venues. A typical session is 10 to 20 minutes at a temperature you can tolerate comfortably. Infrared saunas run cooler, so sessions there often go a little longer.

What cold does

Cold water causes blood vessels near the skin to narrow and lowers tissue temperature. Most people feel less sore and more alert afterward. That's useful after a race, between back-to-back hard days, or during a heavy training block when you just need to feel fresh for tomorrow.

The catch is that inflammation after training is part of how your body adapts. Regular cold plunges immediately after lifting can blunt some of the strength and muscle gains you're training for.

A simple contrast session

If you have both available, this is an easy starting point:

  • 10 to 15 minutes of sauna
  • 2 to 3 minutes of cold plunge, breathing slowly through the nose
  • A few minutes of rest at room temperature
  • Repeat for 2 to 3 rounds total

Finish on cold if you want to feel alert. Finish with a warm shower if you're heading to bed soon. Drink water between rounds, since you'll sweat more than you realize.

When to use cold, and when to skip it

Good days for cold: after long runs, after interval or conditioning sessions, after a race simulation, and during race week when your only goal is showing up fresh.

Days to skip cold: right after heavy lifting, especially during a strength block. If you want to plunge on a lifting day, wait at least 4 to 6 hours, or use the sauna on its own instead.

Race week and race day

Keep everything familiar during race week. If you've never used a cold plunge, race week isn't the time to start. If you already use one, short and easy sessions in the final few days are fine. After the race, a cold plunge or cold shower that evening and a gentle sauna a day or two later is a popular way to take the edge off the soreness from sleds, lunges and wall balls.

No plunge at home?

You don't need expensive equipment. A cold shower for 2 to 3 minutes, a bathtub with a few bags of ice, or a local gym day pass with a sauna will get you most of the benefit. Consistency and sleep still matter far more than any single recovery tool.

What to bring to the recovery session

Getting warm quickly after cold water matters. A heavy layer like the Run. Station. Repeat. is the easiest thing to throw on between rounds, and the AeroShell Lightweight Warmup Jacket works well when you're walking home from the gym. Keep water or electrolytes in the 24oz Insulated Shaker Bottle, and pack towels and a change of clothes in the 8-Station 50L Gym & Shoe Duffle so wet gear stays separate.

Use heat to relax, use cold when you need to feel fresh, and keep both away from the sessions you're trying to get stronger from.

guides.title: What to Eat Before a Hybrid Fitness Race: Race-Day Nutrition and Hydration Plan
guides.summary: A practical plan for the dinner before, race-morning breakfast, the last hour in the start area, and what to do about fuel during an 8-run, 8-station race, plus how to rehydrate and refuel afterward.
faqs: How long before a hybrid race should I eat breakfast?

Most athletes eat a carb-focused breakfast 2.5 to 3 hours before their start time. That gives you time to digest while still topping up energy. If your wave starts very early, a smaller meal 90 minutes before often works better than skipping food.
Do I need to eat or drink during the race?

Most age-group racers finishing in 60 to 100 minutes don't need solid food during the race. Sipping water at the hydration station is usually enough. Athletes racing longer, or in hot venues, may benefit from a small carb drink or gel, but test it in training first.
Should I carb-load before a hybrid race?

A full multi-day carb load isn't necessary for most racers, but eating a bit more carbohydrate than usual the day before helps you start with full energy stores. Keep foods familiar and avoid very high-fiber or greasy meals.
What should I eat after the race?
Within an hour or two, have a meal with carbohydrates and protein, and keep drinking fluids with some sodium. A shake with protein and fruit is an easy option if you're not hungry yet.
guides.body_html:
You can put months into your running, sled work and wall balls and still have a rough race because of what you ate that morning. Nutrition for an hour-plus hybrid race isn't complicated, but it does reward a bit of planning.

This guide walks through the day before, race morning, the waiting area, the race itself and the hours afterward. Treat it as a starting point and test everything in training first.

The day before

Eat normal, familiar meals with a little more carbohydrate than usual: rice, pasta, potatoes, bread, oats and fruit. You don't need a giant pasta dinner. Keep fiber, fat and spicy food moderate in the evening so your stomach is calm in the morning. Drink water steadily through the day, and add a pinch of salt or an electrolyte drink if you sweat heavily or you're racing somewhere warm.

Race morning breakfast

Aim to eat about 2.5 to 3 hours before your start. Simple, carb-focused options work well:

  • Oatmeal with banana and honey
  • A bagel or toast with jam or peanut butter
  • Rice with eggs, if that's what you normally eat

Add a moderate amount of protein if it sits well with you, and have your usual coffee if you normally drink it. Race morning isn't the day to try a new pre-workout or a double espresso you've never had.

The last hour before your wave

Start areas often run late. Bring a small snack, like a banana, a few dried dates or a simple energy bar, and eat it 30 to 60 minutes before your start. Sip water, but don't chug a full bottle right before the corral. A small amount of sodium in your drink can help if the venue is hot.

During the race

Most racers finishing in 60 to 100 minutes don't need solid food. A few sips of water at the hydration point after the middle stations is usually enough. If you're racing longer, sweat a lot, or have had energy dips late in training simulations, try a gel or carb drink around the halfway mark in practice first. Your stomach takes a beating on burpee broad jumps and wall balls, so less is often more.

After you cross the line

Within an hour or two, have a proper meal with both carbohydrate and protein, and keep drinking fluids with some sodium. If you're not hungry yet, a protein shake with fruit is an easy start. Keep eating normally over the next day, since your legs will still be repairing from the sleds and lunges.

Practice it in training

Run at least two race simulations with your exact race-morning plan: same breakfast, same timing, same snack. That's the only way to know your stomach will cooperate on the day.

Gear that makes fueling easier

Pre-mix your electrolyte drink or post-race shake in the 24oz Double-Wall Insulated Shaker Bottle so it stays cold through the wait. Pack your breakfast backup, snacks and a change of clothes in the 8-Station 50L Gym & Shoe Duffle. If you're running your aerobic base by heart rate, the Zone 2 All Week, Redline Weekend Race Tee fits the plan, and the AeroShell Lightweight Warmup Jacket keeps you warm in a chilly start area.

Keep it simple, keep it familiar, and save the experiments for training day.

guides.title: How to Train for Your First Hybrid Fitness Race: An 8-Week Plan for Beginners
guides.summary: A realistic 8-week plan for first-time hybrid racers: how to split your week between running, station practice and strength, what a race simulation should look like, and how to taper so you show up fresh.
faqs: Is 8 weeks enough to train for a first hybrid fitness race?

If you can already run 5km without stopping and you train a few times a week, 8 weeks is enough to finish comfortably. The goal for a first race is to get to the line healthy and familiar with every station, not to chase a fast time.
How many days a week should I train?
Four to five sessions a week works for most beginners: two runs, one or two strength and station sessions, and one combined session that mixes running with stations. Keep at least one full rest day.
Do I need access to a sled and SkiErg?

It helps, but it isn't required. Heavy prowler pushes, band-resisted walks and rope pulls can stand in for the sleds, and a rower or assault bike can cover the erg work if your gym has no SkiErg. Try to get on the real equipment a few times before race day.
How should I taper in the last week?

Cut your total training volume by roughly half in the final week while keeping a little intensity, like a few short race-pace efforts early in the week. Rest or walk the two days before the race, sleep well and eat familiar food.
guides.body_html:
Signing up for your first hybrid race is exciting right up until you read the format: eight 1km runs, each followed by a station. SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges and wall balls. It sounds like a lot, and it is, but it's very finishable with two months of steady work.

This plan assumes you can already run about 5km without stopping and train three or four times a week. If you're not there yet, spend a few weeks building up your running first.

How the 8 weeks are laid out

  • Weeks 1 to 3, build the base. Easy running, learning each station, and general strength.
  • Weeks 4 to 6, add the hard part. Running straight off stations, longer combined sessions and one half-race simulation.
  • Week 7, full rehearsal. One near-complete simulation with your race kit and race breakfast.
  • Week 8, taper. Less volume, a little sharpness, lots of sleep.

A typical training week

  • Easy run (30 to 50 min). Conversational pace. This is where most of your fitness comes from. Our Zone 2 heart rate guide explains how to keep it truly easy.
  • Interval run. Something like 5 to 8 rounds of 1km at a pace you could hold for the whole race, with 90 seconds of rest.
  • Strength and stations. Squats, lunges, deadlifts or carries, plus 15 to 20 minutes of practice on two or three stations.
  • Combined session. Alternate 1km runs with a station, for example run, 500m row, run, 25 wall balls, run, 100m farmers carry. Start with three rounds and build to five or six.
  • Rest day. Walk, stretch, sleep. You get fitter when you recover, not while you train.

Learning the stations

Beginners lose the most time on the sleds, the burpee broad jumps and the wall balls. For the sleds, keep your arms long, your hips low and take short, quick steps. For burpee broad jumps, find a steady rhythm you can hold for the full 80m rather than sprinting the first 20m. For wall balls, break the reps into sets you know you can repeat, like 10s or 15s, before you get to the point of failing.

If you want more detail, see our guides on sled push and sled pull technique and pacing the final 100 wall balls.

Your race simulations

In week 5 or 6, do a half simulation: four runs and four stations at race effort. In week 7, do six to eight rounds, using the same shoes, shirt and breakfast you plan to use on race day. Write down your split for each run and each station. It will tell you where to save energy and give you realistic targets.

The taper

In the final week, cut your training roughly in half. Keep one short session with a few race-pace efforts early in the week, then walk or rest for the last two days. You won't lose fitness in a week, but you can easily show up tired if you try to squeeze in one more big workout.

Common first-timer mistakes

  • Running the first 1km far too fast because of the crowd and the music.
  • Skipping strength work, then finding the lunges and wall balls brutal on tired legs.
  • Trying a new shoe, new shirt or new breakfast on race day.
  • Never practicing the transition from a station back into running.

Gear for the 8 weeks

For the long combined sessions, a light, breathable top like the Compromised Running Breathable Race Tech Tee keeps you from overheating, and the Run. Station. Repeat. Heavyweight Race Tee is a good everyday training shirt. If you're doing your easy runs by heart rate, the Zone 2 All Week, Redline Weekend Tee suits the plan. Bring water or electrolytes in the 24oz Insulated Shaker Bottle, carry your shoes and a change of clothes in the 8-Station 50L Gym & Shoe Duffle, and keep the AeroShell Lightweight Warmup Jacket on in the start area until your wave is called.

When you're ready to plan race day itself, our first-race outfit checklist and race-morning nutrition plan cover the rest.

guides.title: Doubles Hybrid Race Strategy: How to Split the Stations With Your Partner
guides.summary: How to plan a doubles race with your partner: who takes which reps, when to swap, how to pace the runs together, and how to practice handoffs so you don't lose time in the transitions.
faqs: How does doubles work in a hybrid fitness race?

In the doubles format, both partners run every 1km together, and the work at each station can be split however you like, as long as only one person works at a time. That makes your plan for splitting the stations a big part of your result.
Should we split every station 50/50?

Usually not. The fastest teams split the work based on strengths. A stronger partner might take more of the sled push, while a lighter, faster partner might take more burpee broad jumps or erg meters. Just make sure nobody arrives at the next run completely wrecked.
How often should we swap on the stations?

Short, frequent swaps work best on the hardest stations. Many teams swap every 10 wall balls, every 250m on the ergs, and every half length or full length on the sleds. Longer turns mean fewer handoffs but more fatigue.
Who should set the pace on the runs?
The slower runner on the day should set the pace. Running together is required, and the faster partner pushing too hard on the run usually costs the team more time at the next station than it saves.
guides.body_html:
Doubles is the best way to try a hybrid race for the first time, and it's often more fun than racing alone. You still run all eight 1km runs, but you run them together, and you share the work at every station. The catch is that how you split that work can make a difference of several minutes.

Here's how to build a plan with your partner before race day, so you're not negotiating in the middle of the sled push.

Start with an honest strengths list

Sit down together and rate each of you on the eight stations: SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges and wall balls. Be honest. Most pairs find they have one partner who is stronger on the heavy, grinding stations and one who is better on the erg and bodyweight work. Your plan should lean into that.

A sample split

  • SkiErg and row. Swap every 250m. Short turns let you both work near your best pace.
  • Sled push and sled pull. Swap every length, with the stronger partner taking an extra length if needed.
  • Burpee broad jumps. Swap every 10 to 20 meters. These get ugly fast, so keep turns short.
  • Farmers carry. Split it 50/50, or let the partner with the better grip take more.
  • Sandbag lunges. Swap every 20 to 25 meters to protect both of your legs for the finish.
  • Wall balls. Swap every 10 reps. Fast, clean handoffs here are worth a lot of time.

Treat this as a starting point, then adjust after a training session together.

Pace the runs for the slower partner

You have to run together, so the runs go at the pace of whoever is more tired. The faster runner's job is to stay calm and talk, not pull ahead. Go out conservatively on the first two runs. A steady, shared pace almost always beats a fast start followed by a struggle.

Practice the handoffs

Most time in doubles is lost in transitions: the wall ball that rolls away, the confusion over who goes next, the partner who wasn't ready. Agree on simple words like "two more" and "go," decide where the resting partner stands, and practice swapping the ball, the erg handles and the sled rope at least a few times in training.

Do one full partner simulation

Three to four weeks out, run a full or near-full simulation together using your plan. Time each station and note where one of you was waiting or one of you was cooked. Adjust the split from what actually happened, not from what you guessed. Our 1km split pacing guide can help you set realistic run targets for the pair.

Recover together, too

Both of you will be sore the next day, especially from the sleds and lunges. Our 48-hour recovery protocol walks through cold plunge, compression and easy movement timing after the race.

Look the part as a team

Matching shirts make it easier to spot each other in a busy Roxzone and look great in the finish photos. Popular doubles pairings include the Sled Push Enthusiast Tee with the I Don't Need To Defend My Sled Push Tee, or two Wall Balls & Bad Decisions Pump Cover Tees with the matching Wall Balls & Bad Decisions Hoodie for the walk to the start. Throw an AeroShell Lightweight Warmup Jacket over the top if your venue is cold. For more ideas, see our matching doubles shirts guide.
